name: Guard
description: The one place the shop learns about things it would otherwise never hear: application errors that end up in a log file nobody opens, and who changed what in the admin. Later: watched invariants and blocking — each switched on separately.

settings.label: Collect application errors
settings.help: Costs nothing in ordinary life: it only runs when something has already gone wrong. A 500 on the storefront otherwise goes to storage/logs, which nobody opens — so as far as the shop is concerned it never happened.

settings.label: Record from this level
settings.help: Warnings include deprecations and other noise a working shop produces anyway; errors are things that actually failed.

settings.label: Ignore anything containing
settings.help: One per line, matched anywhere in the message or the exception's class. For the one noisy thing a shop cannot fix and has decided to live with — not a way to make the list look tidy.

settings.label: Keep errors for, days
settings.help: Counted from when a group was last seen, so a problem that is still happening is never pruned. 0 keeps everything, which is how this table becomes the biggest one in the database.

settings.label: Check the invariants nightly
settings.help: The statements each module makes about what must be true — no negative stock, a total that adds up, a counter within its limit. You can also press the button on the Invariants screen at any time.

settings.label: At most this many problems per check
settings.help: A check that finds its limit's worth stops there and says "at least". The point of the screen is to tell you something is wrong, and the first fifty say that as well as the first fifty thousand.

options.watch: Watch — record what it would block, refuse nobody

settings.label: Blocking
settings.help: Watching is the default deliberately: read the Blocking screen for a week first, because the addresses it lists are your own traffic and nobody knows what that looks like until they have looked. A request that presents valid credentials is never touched in any mode — a signed-in session, an API token, 1C, a payment callback.

settings.label: Block after this many refusals
settings.help: One number for all of them — wrong passwords, refused forms, unknown API tokens — because "ten refusals in ten minutes" is something a person can reason about and four separate thresholds are not. What kind they were is on the screen; it just is not what decides.

settings.label: …counted within, minutes
settings.help: The window the refusals are counted in. Long windows catch the patient attacker and also the customer who forgot their password on Monday and again on Friday.

settings.label: Block for, minutes
settings.help: Multiplied by how many times the address has been back — coming back after being let in is the clearest evidence there is that the first block was right — and never longer than a week. An automatic block that outlives the attack is indistinguishable from a customer who cannot reach the shop.

settings.label: Never block these
settings.help: One address or network per line (203.0.113.9, 10.0.0.0/8). The office, the warehouse, the monitoring service — anything whose absence you would notice a day late. A private or reserved address is never blocked automatically anyway: seeing every visitor as one address is what a shop behind an untrusted proxy looks like, and the first automatic block would then shut the whole shop.

settings.label: Keep lifted blocks for, days
settings.help: Counted from when a block stopped standing, so nothing that is still blocking is ever pruned. The row of an address that came back is what tells the next block it is not the first time. 0 keeps everything.

settings.label: CAPTCHA
settings.help: The last cheap layer, under the honeypot, the form-age stamp and the rate limits that are always on. The built-in one asks a small sum drawn as a picture and needs no account anywhere; another module can add reCAPTCHA or Turnstile and it appears in this list.

settings.label: Ask on these forms
settings.help: Per form on purpose: a CAPTCHA is a tax on every real customer, so it goes on the one form that is being spammed rather than on the shop. Nothing ticked means nobody is ever asked.

settings.label: Never ask these customer groups
settings.help: Staff are never asked at all — somebody signed into the admin has proved more than a picture could. This is for the customers you already trust: a wholesale buyer placing their fifth order this week should not be doing arithmetic.

settings.label: The answer is valid for, minutes
settings.help: Long enough to fill in a form, short enough that a captured answer is worthless later. Each answer works once whatever this says.

options.offered: Offered — each manager decides, unless their group is ticked below
options.required: Required of every member of staff

settings.label: Two-factor authentication for staff
settings.help: A password is the whole of the admin panel: the catalogue, the orders and every customer's address. Requiring a second factor never locks anybody out — somebody who must have one and has none is sent to the enrolment page instead of the page they asked for, which is the same thirty seconds they would have spent voluntarily. What CAN lock a shop out is a lost phone with no recovery codes written down, and the way back from that is `php artisan guard:two-factor <email> --off`.

settings.label: …and required of these permission groups
settings.help: Read only while the setting above says "offered", where it means "…and for these it is not optional". The people who can change prices, refund money or edit staff are worth insisting on; a warehouse worker who marks parcels as shipped may not be. Nothing ticked means nobody is forced.

options.offered: Offered — each customer decides, unless their group is ticked below

settings.label: Two-factor authentication for customers
settings.help: Off out of the box: an account area that grows a security page nobody asked for is a support question, and a customer's own account is theirs to protect. Requiring it of everybody is a real setting and rarely the right one — it is a hurdle in front of every returning buyer. Requiring it of a GROUP usually is: a wholesale account with a credit line and a saved address book is worth more to steal than a shop's own login.

settings.label: …and required of these customer groups
settings.help: Read only while the setting above says "offered". The wholesale tier, the dealers, anybody whose account can spend money it has not paid yet. Nothing ticked means nobody is forced.

permissions.name: guard.revert
permissions.label: Undo changes from the audit trail
